utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me greet the Prosecution as well as the witness, the Defence counsel, and the accused. We are now going to proceed with the cross-examination of the witness, General Pringle. Before we do so, I'm first going to give the floor to Mr. Registrar who is going to give us an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The OTP has submitted a response to exhibits tendered by 4D for witness Ray Lane. The list submitted by OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 706. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With respect to the application made for General Petkovic by Ms. Alaburic for additional time, notwithstanding her application for a certification to appeal our previous decision, yesterday Ms. Alaburic asked for additional time. The Chamber considered the matter and has decided to maintain its previous decision by allowing to Ms. Alaburic one hour, but, of course, the other Defence counsel are free to offer any time they wish to Ms. Alaburic. The Trial Chamber saw that the 23 page expert report includes 80 paragraphs and that it is a factual report related to documents coming from the former Yugoslavia and from the HVO. As a consequence, the Trial Chamber believes that if the Defence want to introduce exhibits or evidence to support its case, it can do so later on when it calls its own witnesses. This being said, we maintain, we uphold our previous decision. We'll issue a written decision on the application for certification to appeal. With respect now to the time left to Ms. Nozica, she has 16 more minutes. We have deducted the time she used yesterday at the beginning, she had 30 minutes plus 15 minutes offered to her by the Prlic Defence. Let me also add for the transcript that when I said that the witness had drafted a report, the report was a normative report and not a factual report. Ms. Nozica, you have the floor for the 16 minutes that are left to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day to everyone in the courtroom. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll start with my cross-examination immediately so as not to waste any more time. Sir, you compiled another report, as far as I'm aware, but in order to get to your answer as rapidly as possible please have a look at P09211 which is in my pink binder. It is the fourth document from the top.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you confirm the number? Did you say 9221?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. It's down here, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: 9211. It's the fourth from the bottom. I apologise. I provided you with the wrong information. It's the fourth document from the bottom in the binder. Have you found the document now?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I believe you know what this is about, so could you please tell the Court what this document is, in fact, about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's entitled "Structure of the HVO Armed Forces."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you compile or draft this analysis and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Then the information I had was incorrect. Thank you. There is nothing I want to ask you about this document in that case. In item 47 of your report -- could we help the witness? Do you have your report before you? If not, could the Prosecution binder be provided to the witness?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. I haven't got the two files that I had yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please have a look at item 47 in your report.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have paragraph 47.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In item 47, you mentioned the obligation to train soldiers, to teach them about the Geneva Conventions and about the obligations derived from those conventions, and also how to treat civilians, prisoners of war, and the wounded. In the penultimate sentence of this paragraph, you say "That in the documents I have been given by the Prosecution, I saw nothing that had to do with the requirement to train soldiers in their legal obligations and responsibilities under the international laws of war." In the course of the examination-in-chief, the Prosecution showed you a number of documents. There are many documents, in fact, and in those documents it can be seen that HVO soldiers were informed of their legal obligations in relation to the Geneva Conventions and this was done through the line of command or through education. Am I right in saying this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it would be executed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll be showing you a number of documents that you haven't yet seen, a number of orders, in fact, in which soldiers are being directly informed of their obligations and legal obligations in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. We'll go through these documents now. The first one is P2877. It's a document in my binder, P02877. It's the seventh document from the top in my binder. Let's have a look at this document. It's dated the 21st of June 1993. Mr. Blaskic signed the document, the command of the central Bosnian operative zone in Vitez. It says, "All -- it's for all brigade commanders and wardens of military prisons." It's called the relation or the attitude towards war prisoners, and it says, "On the basis of the Geneva Conventions of the 12th of August 1949 regulating the treatment of prisoners of war, I hereby order, item 1, treatment of prisoners of war must be humane. I forbid the use of prisoners of war for enforced work." He informs the wardens -- it informs wardens of military prisons about the cases in which prisoners of war can be used and in which cases they can't be used. It draws attention to the fact that an International Tribunal for war crimes has been established, and it will deal with all contraventions of the Geneva Conventions, and 4, it says, "I will hold brigade commanders and military prison wardens responsible for carrying out this order." Sir, in light of your practice, would this be an appropriate way in which soldiers can be informed of their obligations, their legal obligations, pursuant to the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order by Colonel Blaskic to the brigade commanders and military prison wardens saying exactly the right sort of thing, ordering them to effectively comply by the Geneva Conventions and mentioning specific sorts of maltreatment that he is talking about and is drawing their attention to are not to be conducted. That's a good order but that's not the same as training the soldiers in that. So we go back to where I were yesterday. There is giving the order, the next part is ensuring that it happens. And ensuring that it happens would have to involve the recipients of that order down to the lowest levels understanding what it was that they were meant to be doing. So good order, whether it was complied or carried out with, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I'll just ask you about individual orders. You can then say whether this is a good way to inform of the Geneva Conventions, as to whether soldiers were aware of these things, I won't ask you about that. You don't know. You told me you provided your report in accordance with the documentation you were provided with, so we'll just stick to what you yourself have seen and to the documents that I'll be showing you. I haven't got much time left, but I would just like to show you a few such orders to see the time period we are dealing with and to see what members of these units were informed of. Please have a look at P03608 now. It's in the middle of the binder, more or less. Tell me when you've found the document.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is an order issued one month later, signed by Mr. Blaskic, the treatment of prisoners and civilians is the subject. Blaskic is referring to the order of the chief of the Main Staff dated the 20th of July, and he says HVO members must treat prisoners in accordance with international regulations, and especially captured civilians. They must treat soldiers in accordance with these regulations. And item 5, the directly subordinate commanders of persons responsible for me for the execution of this order. It's quite clear that Mr. Blaskic one month after the first order issued a second order, the contents of which are similar. It's on the basis of the chief of the HVO main headquarters, and we can see the following. Does this mean that this commander was following the provisions of the Geneva Conventions? So he wanted these provisions to be respected and as a result, he issued requests on a number of occasions or orders on a number of occasions to ensure that these provisions were in fact respected. Could we put things this way?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's possibly going a little bit far. What this order does is quite correctly Colonel Blaskic has reiterated very much the same order that he gave a month before, to say, to go on to say that that means that he is complying with the Geneva Conventions, is to take it in my opinion too far, because he would have to be satisfied that these orders are being carried out and that none of the sorts of acts that he is forbidding in his order are being carried out. So, again, it's a good order. It's a good written order.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's what I want to hear from you. What did Mr. Blaskic do to determine whether his orders, this one and the prefer one, were respected? Well, that's not part of my examination. Let's just concentrate on this. I'll show you a few more such orders. For the sake of continuity have a look at P06989. In my binder, it's the fourth order from below, from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As you can see it's dated the 1st of December 1993. The subject is POWs and adhering to the Geneva Conventions. Item 2 states the following: Use the commanders of units and organs for propaganda to inform all soldiers of the contents of this order. As you can see, this was provided to everyone in his operative zone. You can see that at the top. Can we say that the commander of this operative zone in fact did what was necessary in this order to inform everyone of their obligations pursuant to the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can say that once again, Colonel Blaskic, several months after issuing the same order, is producing another written order on the same subject. We can say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In your report, you also mentioned obligation to treat wounded enemy prisoners in a certain way and you also mention obligations pursuant to the Geneva Conventions, and then you quote the Geneva Conventions. It's item 47 or paragraph 47 in your report. We don't have to have a look at it now, though. But when you compiled your report, when you were compiling your report, did you see any documents demonstrating how the HVO treated wounded enemy soldiers, and if so, are there any conclusions you can draw as to the extent to which the HVO abided by these obligations pursuant to the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing any reports of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's then have a look at document P02050. It's the fifth document in my binder. Let me know when you've found it.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have a joint order from Bruno Stojic and Petkovic dated the 24th of April 1993. It's at a fairly high level. It says this order is being provided to commanders of operative zones and all commanders and soldiers. The order states the following: When need arises for medical assistance, ensure that your doctors and other medical personnel have access to each injured person at any moment regardless of whether the person is a civilian or member of an enemy unit. Behave towards civilians and prisoners solely in accordance with international conventions and rules. Could you comment on this order?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is a written order by Bruno Stojic saying the right thing, a good, written order.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now finally, let's see how an order of this kind was put into practice and for that let's look at document 2D 566 which should be the second document, 2D 00566. And tell me when you've found it, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a report from the health sector to the Defence department at the -- dated 1993, the 10th of September, where we have a list of wounded members of the BH army sent from the war hospital of the HVO in Mostar to the hospital in Split. And the names of persons are listed here along with the diagnoses, and we have a total of 11 members of the BH army who were in the Mostar war hospital and quite obviously, because the hospital was not able to provide full medical treatment because of the wartime conditions, they were sent further on to the hospital in Split, which is Croatia. Now, can we say that this document is, in fact, a follow-up of the activities to implement the orders issued by Bruno Stojic and Mr. Milivoj Petkovic or rather does it show the conduct towards the wounded, the POWs from enemy armies based on the Geneva Conventions? Of course, you don't have to say whether you know whether this actually happened but let's assume that it did and that what it says in this document is true and correct.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that assumption, this document would indicate to me that Dr. Ivo Sandrk if that's the right pronunciation, is acting in what would appear on the face of it to be a humane and correct manner to these specific prisoners. I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, for the record, I'd like to stress that the name of the person who signed the document is Dr. Ivo Sandrk. Thank you, sir. I think that that has taken up all my 16 minutes that I had at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Following counsel? Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in keeping with your ruling of the 10th of May of this year and in conformity with paragraph 11, I would like to request that my client, General Praljak, be allowed to question the witness. I think that they are extraordinary circumstances as stipulated in paragraph 11 because Mr. Praljak was there on the spot, he has direct knowledge of the situation, and of course he has specialist knowledge with respect to his training and education. I don't think that need be challenged nor do I need to present arguments. So he would be taking the floor now with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you have only one hour? Has nobody given you any extra time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have one hour which we were assigned and 15 minutes ceded from the Pusic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Praljak, you have 75 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, military -- I have waited for 17 months for military topics to come up for discussion in this courtroom. It was my hope that you would be at our disposal for longer, at least five or six hours for myself and General Petkovic so that we could illustrate the very serious wartime problems that we had which would help them in their decision and judgement later on. But as time is short I'd like to ask you, General, to be as brief as possible in your answers to my questions. I shall try and formulate them in such a way to make that possible. But at the outset, let's see what in your report, in your expert report, you dealt with in connection with the HVO. So can you confirm the following. Do you know how many soldiers the HVO had? Let's start off with that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, let's start off with paragraph 2 of my report, where I explain what I was asked to do. I was asked to explain the nature of command and control in military organisations by drawing on personal experience. I was asked to comment on the normal military political interface in general between senior military commanders, civilian defence ministers and commanders in chief, and I was asked to offer professional opinions on the military significance of a number of documents provided by the Prosecution. I do not pretend to be an expert in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we do of course understand that you are not an expert in the HVO, but it seems to us that you held very important positions in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 1993-95 period of time, and during that period, you no doubt had contacts with the both -- with both branches, HVO and ABiH. At the time there must have been several thousand soldiers there. Do you have any idea about the -- an approximate number of soldiers? We are not asking you for a very precise estimate. But in the framework of the federation that was set up under the Dayton agreement, how many soldiers were there, if we take them altogether, Croats plus ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would hesitate to guess at that. I'm generally aware that the HVO was made up of a mixture of regular and irregular troops. I'm generally aware that there were also a number of HV soldiers in Bosnia. I'm generally aware that they were organised into a number of ZPs or operational zones and brigades of varying numbers each. I hesitate to put a number on it but if you want me to put a number on it, shall we say for the sake of argument 50.000? I don't know. I mean -- enough to be conducting a serious war anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. General Praljak, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, not for a moment did I doubt that within the frameworks works of the parameters given you by the Prosecutor that you did not do your utmost to respond and to provide the answers to the questions to the best of your knowledge. I'm not challenging that at all. What I would like to find out is the following. Or rather, I claim that the Prosecution is supplying people with partial documents and is resorting to vivisection in a war by showing a bone here, a bone there, rib bone there, a leg bone there. So I don't mind all your answers, as far as I'm concerned, are very good when you say yes or when you say no. So what we want to see orders, control, and communication, three basic points in wartime. So you've said you can't say exactly how many soldiers the HVO had. Now, if I were to put up a map or a chart, could you draw in four operative zones in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993, for example, would you be capable of doing that? Would you be capable of drawing in the parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina which at that time were under HVO control?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not. Straight off the top of my head, with a bit of research and reminding, I had contact with General Glasnovic in ZP Tomislavgrad, for example, on a number of occasions and I also visited Mostar on a number of occasions, but I wouldn't wish to put a pen to a map and start trying to pretend to know how your HVO districts were delineated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you know what the communication was like between the Main Staff or myself as the commander of the Main Staff of the HVO, between myself and the 4th Posavina operative zone, or the Central Bosnia operative zone, for example, or operative group 2 Kiseljak or Zepce? Did you in any way have any documents or did you do research into the possibility of the Main Staff's communicating with all the subordinate units? If you don't know that will suffice.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm generally aware that you had radio communications, you had telefax communications, you had radio relay communications, you had telephone communications, you had courier communications. In detail I can't tell you, but you had those forms of communications and in the normal event some would be working sometimes and others would not and that's how you would be communicating.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You say telephone communications. What telephone communications did the Grude headquarters have in with Zepce, Kiseljak, Vitez, or Orasje? Do you know whether there were any telephone communications, and if so what kind or fax communication for that matter?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course I can't answer that question in detail. What I do know is that your front lines were interspersed and some of your locations were cut off from others, and therefore telephone communications in some instance probably would have been irregular and in some instances probably non-existent because they ran through other factional war zones and had been cut, but I can't answer your question in detail, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's define it this way: A communication line, let's call it a link between somebody providing information and on the other hand somebody receiving information. That's what we mean by communication. Now, in your division as the commander of a division, within that division, how many communication lines did you have?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be able to communicate by radio, by telephone, by radio relay, by fax, all the sorts of communication systems that I have just described to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In a study at the beginning of the war, compiled at the beginning of the war, I happened to read and you'll at the me if I'm right or not that the 101st Marine Division or sometimes referred to as the 1st Division, which has about 20.000 troops when it's at full strength, at a time of action has 27 .000 communication lines within its unit, 27.000 communication lines. Everybody communicating with everybody else. Now, would that piece of information be correct or roughly correct to the best of your knowledge? And my second question is this: Do you know when I was up on a hill or at my headquarters, how many communication lines I could have had with my troops and units?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, General to answer your first question, I'm not an expert in the marine division and 27.000 communication lines rather depends on how you define communication lines. If that's one person includes one person talking to another, as well as all the other systems, you possibly could define it like that but I can't comment on that. As to the second question, I wasn't with you up on your hill so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in the famous three member or like the holy trinity, if we can put it that way in modern times, these three parts of the army and the control and command of the army and communications, so control, command, and communications being the three elements, communication, is that a vital part of good quality control and command, whether they -- whether we are referring to technical communication or whether communication is carried out in the sense of the recipient receiving correct information, which would mean that the commander can be in charge of an operation, whether an offensive or defensive operation, that they can be in command of the army. So my question is this, let me repeat it: Is the existence of a communication system vital for a modern military authority and control and command?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said in my report, communications are an essential part of command and control. You cannot execute command and you cannot coordinate control if you have an ineffective communication system.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: One of the areas you dealt with is -- well hypothetically, if a commander knew or were to know and so on. But let's look at feedback information about an event now. You learn about some houses being on fire, and you have to establish who set fire to those houses and launch an investigation, and before you make a decision to punish the perpetrators, you must investigate to see who it was who committed the crime and where it was committed, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, as far as information goes, General, I think we all know this from history, the crime in My Lai in Vietnam was uncovered two years after it had been committed because one of the members, one of the participants in that event, had drunk too much alcohol in a bar and then told the man sitting next to him about the event who -- and the man happened to be an intelligence officer, a US intelligence officer. Do you know about that, that that's how crimes came to be uncovered, the crimes that happened in My Lai in Vietnam and that this was two years after the event?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the incident you're talking about. I do not have the knowledge that you have just put on the table about how it came to be in the public forum.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. But we have another example, Abu Ghraib, the military prison, for example, this is in more recent times, in Iraq. Do you know that what happened in that prison there was uncovered, came to light, because a man in England when developing photographs saw what he saw, and then took those photographs to the press and to television? So that event was not uncovered by the internal organs of the army, it was uncovered in a photograph shop, photographic shop, by this man who sent them, sent the incriminated material to the press and television? Do you know about that? That was quite recent.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the Abu Ghraib incident. I can't comment on your allegations as to how it came to become public.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'll quote another example because it's very important. This is a very important point to bring crimes to light and then punish the perpetrators and it's especially important for me, the people around me, and for this Court in general. Several months ago, for instance, the German papers published the fact that German professional soldiers in Afghanistan arranged human bones and made sculptures out of them, and all this happened five years ago and it was uncovered once again quite by chance when a photographer found the material and sent it to the media. So these are ways in which sometimes very serious crimes are uncovered, crimes perpetrated by soldiers from professional armies. Of course, it doesn't happen everywhere but I have quoted just a few examples, so are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the last example you have given. In general, I understand the point you're trying to make. It is not unknown that incidents happen and they come to light later on. Specific incidents. I would agree with that. That is possible. The general execution of such incidents particularly when they are on the television on a daily basis is rather more difficult to cover up, obviously. So it depends on the event and the specificity of what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, General. Now I'd like to try and compare the concept of army. It's vulgar nominalism, where under the term "army" or concept "army," all forms of organisation are attempted to be included, people bearing weapons. So I'm going to ask you the following. Do you know that in 1992, the HVO, that is to say the beginning of 1992, was established or rather a group of volunteers had gathered together at municipality level in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that that was the start?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll take your word for that, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that people and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General, the witness, I take your word for it is not really an answer. He asks whether you know. If you do not yourself know, you just say, no, I don't know. But this, "I take your word for it" means that you believe the accused which is not of interest to the Chamber whether you believe him or not. It's just what you know that you are to tell us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise. Specifically, the answer to your question is no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right. My next question: Do you know that the municipal authorities, through municipal staffs of the HVO, were in command of that army. So it was the municipal authorities through various staffs, that -- the local ones, that the army was commanded?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said to you at the beginning, I'm not an expert in the HVO. I am generally aware that the HVO had a command chain that ran from the president down through the Main Staff down to the operational zones and brigades. I'm also generally aware that the HVO was a -- had a civil and a military dimension to it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, we'll come back to structures of control and command in due course, and during your many years of experience, you dealt with von Scharnhorst and Clausewitz and others, and you know that the parameters of a society determine what kind of army and war a country is going to have. So if you say, "I did know that or I did not know that," that will help me, and I'll just get through the elements that I wish to raise. I'm not dealing with formal establishment on paper; although, we'll look at paper and documents later on too. But just in general terms, practical terms now, tell me, do you know that the number of volunteers at that time, who had rallied together within the HVO was 35 to 40 per cent, or rather 35 to 40 per cent of those people purchased weapons with their own money? Is that something you knew about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that almost throughout the war, it was the municipalities who financed the brigades established in those municipalities, so it was the municipal authorities which financed the brigades, the Livno Brigade, the Posusje Brigades, it was Livno financing that one, Tomislavgrad would finance the Tomislavgrad Brigade, and so on. So are you aware of that that throughout the war, the brigades were mostly financed by the municipalities themselves?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the detailed financial arrangements of how the HVO was financed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, sir, do you know that those municipalities would collect that money, not by engaging in any economic activities but on the basis of taxes from people, the brothers and sisters of those same fighters or warriors who were in France, Switzerland, working there or any other country, so they would set aside a monthly sum which the guest workers abroad paid in and then this was distributed to the soldiers in the form of a salary? Is that something you might have known about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was generally aware that money was flowing back from the Croatian diaspora. In the detail you put it, no I wasn't aware of that. As I keep saying to you, General, I'm not an expert in the detailed organisation of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, please understand me. All these are essential elements, vital elements, which we have to understand in order to arrive at something which is called control and command. If we do not know in exact terms how things stood and the true establishment, the state of the soul of morale, discipline, the ability to punish and so on, then I'm sure you'll agree with me that we won't be able to understand control and command and how that army was commanded. So I'm going to ask you some more questions along those lines. Do you know that because different municipalities had different revenues and paid out different salaries, on the basis of the documents you looked at provided to you by the Prosecution, do you know how many -- how much rebellion there was or how many rebellions there were when one set of soldiers saw that another set of soldiers had 100 euros more in their salaries? Did you come across problems like that in the documents that you were shown?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I was focused on command and control in its classic sense, the flow of orders down through the responsible chain of command, whether it was reasonable to expect people to know of events and where they did know of events make an assessment of the actions they took on those events. The sorts of detail you're going into now was way beyond anything I was asked to look at.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I'll try and be as brief as possible in this area. Now, tell me, in the documents you studied, did you come across any possibility whereby the Main Staff commander, his deputy or any of the other people here, could do anything significant if 500 conscripts from Herzegovina left the territory or in classical terms in fact deserted? On the basis of the documents you were given, was there any realistic possibility for any sanctions to be taken against these people, 500, 1.000, 5.000? What could these accused here, or I, in the Main Staff, do to punish those people? What could I do with that organisation? Some people called it the state. If any member of the group would lay down his arms and cross the border and leave, would anything like that be possible in England, in America, in the army you were in?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm generally aware from the documents I read that there was a working command and control system that ran from the Main Staff down through the chain of command. I'm also generally aware that there were legal provisions and rules laid out in a doctrine. I'm also generally aware that there were disciplinary codes and punishments that I have also read about. So I'm satisfied that there was a working military system. What you could have done in the specific instance you talk about of soldiers deserting, I don't know, but that would have been very much up to you, your military code, your military system, and your military chain of command, which you had.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, you say -- read through the documents that state that things were functional. I'll ask you something outside the framework of what we call sociology. I'll compare two systems now. I just want a scientific analysis. Let's take a hypothetical country, E, somewhere in the east. Is it correct to say that it has a billion, that the population is one billion, that they have the right to vote, it's a social system of the western kind, a market economy, educational system is functional. Do you know of any such country E in the east?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Population of a billion?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. India, let's say India. It has a market economy, the right to vote, there is no gender discrimination, no religious discrimination, France, Switzerland, and your country share these characteristics. That's what's on paper, as you say. That's what you find in legal documents that pertain to those countries. In the social sense, whether it comes to the functioning of such societies, would France, Switzerland, and England and this country, let's say India, function in the same way or any other countries that have identical laws, the social situation in those countries is nevertheless radically different. It's like the difference between night and day. Is what I am saying correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're saying that all countries are different. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because well, when you read through some papers, well that's one thing. I'll go back to the JNA now. When you read through some legal documents, can you draw the conclusion as to what the actual situation is in a certain country, as to how the system actually functions, or is the way the system functions a problem that's far more difficult than the problem of you seeing certain legal documents? Are you familiar with such a problem in the light of the way in which armies organise, for example?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, general, let me try and turn a mask of generalities into something more specific which is maybe easier to exemplify. Let's say I read a JNA doctrine document on the international laws of war and Geneva Conventions, and let's say I read a document that says we, the country in question, have signed up to these documentations. Then I would make the working assumption that that's what they intend and that's what they intend to do. Notwithstanding the fact that the country in question may not be the same as my country, France, India, or any of the other mass of countries you have specified.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So this is an item that or an issue I'd like to discuss in fact. We don't have to have a dispute about doctrine, but in the former Yugoslavia, there were books that were published on the role of the Communist League, the socialist association, and then there was the role of the SFRY armed forces, the JNA, the Territorial Defence and so on and so forth. My question is as follows: Do you know that the role of the armed forces in Yugoslavia, apart from defending the territory and territorial integrity of the country, was also to protect the political system by having recourse to all means, so we are talking about the Communist Party as well and it had to protect Yugoslavia from being destroyed by using all means? Were you familiar with the fact that such a political role was in fact one of the key roles that the JNA had to play?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the fact that the JNA's key role was the Territorial Defence of the nation and I'm generally aware what -- it had what I would describe as an internal security role.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, you have appeared here as an expert witness on two occasions, in the Dubrovnik case and in the Vukovar case. Was the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia threatened in Dubrovnik and Vukovar or was this an act of violence, an act of aggression? Was the integrity of Yugoslavia under threat or was this the response of the JNA, the reaction of the JNA, to democratic forces within Yugoslavia and the right of people to self-determination after secession?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Until secession.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think to give you a view on that question would be way beyond the remit that I am here as an expert witness and the subjects on which I'm here to comment on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I understand, General. But you've read through some documents, you say that what the JNA stated about the Geneva Conventions is great. That's your conclusion. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that the JNA doctrine on the international laws of armed conflict and the Geneva Conventions and their application, as pronounced in JNA doctrine, appeared to me to be a comprehensive, well written, and thoroughly good document, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I agree. Great document. But let's go back to the application of that document, General. The application of the document involves Mostar, Dubrovnik, Vukovar, Zadar, Sibenik, and everything else that we have here in The Hague. The application of such a perfect doctrine is something that we can see in these courtrooms and on two occasions you were also involved in some judgements. There were high level officials who implemented this doctrine. I think everyone is aware of this. My question is as follows: Wouldn't it be better for the HVO not to have JNA officers amongst its ranks or rather not a significant number of them, because the application of the doctrine, as they understood it, would have led to the same results that we had in Vukovar, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sarajevo and Mostar, et cetera? And now for my fundamental question, well, first, my question was wouldn't it have been better not to have a significant number of JNA officers in the HVO but also is it clear that anything can be put down on paper? Isn't it clear that what is stated on paper provides a feeble basis for drawing conclusions as to what actually happens in reality in wartime situations? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the Judges find it a bit difficult to follow the theory you're trying to outline. You seem to say that maybe it would have been better for the HVO, if the ABiH and others not to have amongst their ranks any officers from the former JNA. Is that the question you're trying to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first question is very clear, Your Honours. It's a hypothetical. If we have a certain doctrine, and if that doctrine had the effects, the results we have seen, my question is then wouldn't it have been better not to have officers who followed the doctrine, and as a result of that doctrine, there were certain results? That's my first question, General, and then I'll put my second question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, can you answer this extremely complex question, but we see the point of that question, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll try. General, on a number of occasions in this Court, I have quoted the good General Patton: Giving the order is the easy part. Making it happen is more difficult. So I agree that having the doctrine is one thing. Teaching it, educating people in it, exercising it, and ensuring it is executed is another thing. But that's where the chain of command and the responsible officers and the whole military system comes into play. To leap from it's all right to have a good doctrine like the JNA had, and then point the finger at a number of atrocities and make the huge conclusion that therefore everybody in the JNA does not abide by their doctrine and therefore should not be in the HVO is, I would have thought, a step in logic too far and one to which I would not ascribe based on the theory you're trying to put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may go on a bit, I think it is a duty of the Chamber, Mr. Praljak, as guardian of the fairness of procedure and the interests of all, that I warned you, because you're making a very strange argument. You are saying look, the JNA had wonderful texts but they did the opposite so the texts are not worth anything. The Prosecution says that you had perhaps some good texts, and some Defence counsel have brought forward texts which are also good texts, and are far -- and the question then remains open what was the application. I think this discrepancy between the good text and the bad application, as you tell the Chamber happens with the JNA, might give the idea that it was the same with the HVO, good texts and bad application. And I think it's a dangerous course, it's a dangerous strategy. You, not being a lawyer, can perhaps not see it, but I think it is our duty to warn you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I be of some assistance, Your Honour, and I don't wish to interrupt the proceedings, but I think where we might have gone astray a little bit was when General Praljak quite rightly asked a question with respect of about 500 deserters, and the realistic possibility, and that was the terms he used, what the realistic possibility was. I noticed that the general sort of avoided answering the questions head on. He went back to his old mantra, where there is documents -- there is a chain of command and so on and so forth. While all his other answers were that clearly he's not an expert in the HVO, and it's quite clear that he doesn't know the situation on the ground. And I think perhaps if the questions could be elicited with respect to what does he actually know about the realistic possibilities on the ground, that's what General Praljak was rather frustrated and which is where he went off on this line of questioning. But it's quite obvious that the gentleman does not know the realistic possibility that a commander had on the ground which is why he reverts to what he does know, which is this is what was on the documents, and perhaps if we could take an early break and maybe have an opportunity to reflect a little bit, I know we almost are in into -- we are in an hour, that might be -- that might be of -- quite appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should -- we still have ten minutes before the break or 20 minutes before the break, 20 minutes. Please proceed, Mr. Praljak. The Trial Chamber has explained to you what sort of direction you've adopted, what sort of way you're going into, but it's your problem. If you're wasting time, it's your problem. Please proceed. Unless, unless we haven't got the point of what you're trying to establish. It's also possible that we haven't quite understood what you're trying to establish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I'm not wasting my time. And I'm not afraid of these legal possibilities you have referred to. All I'm trying to do, is always the same thing with all witnesses. All the good and all the evil, everything that is fine and that is not fine, everything that happens in space and time, is something that happens in reality. And I just want to demonstrate the following through my second question. I want to show that you can't get involved in a reduction of reality and then draw conclusions on that reality, so when the General had certain papers in front of him and when he came to certain conclusions, this is a different question, that relates to the previous one, but when it is said that an excellent JNA document on the Geneva Conventions doesn't provide any results in the field, quite the contrary, then my question is quite simple. Is it essential when looking into the reality, into facts, to see how things actually were, regardless of whether we are dealing with the HVO or orders that were issued or which were then respected or not respected.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is is this proof that anything can be put down on paper and the fact that something has been put down on paper doesn't entitle one to conclude that certain things happened in a certain way? That concerns the JNA, the HVO, the ABiH, et cetera, et cetera. Is it correct that there can be a complete discrepancy between what you have on paper and the facts, whether the facts are positive or negative?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that. That's why I was fairly guarded with my answers to the first counsel's questions where she showed me some excellent written orders. I have no idea whether they were executed in the proper manner or not. So in that respect, General, I agree with you. I go back to the statement giving the order is one thing, making it happen is more difficult.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, I completely agree with you and that is what I'm saying. The easiest thing is to draft an order and to expect the order to be quite simply implemented, and that leads to us the idea of society and organisation, et cetera. But have a look at P04235, P04235. This is a document that has already been shown to the Chamber. It's a document from Prozor and Rama dated the 6th of August 1993. At the time I was the commander of the HVO Main Staff. And I asked the staff to gather information on the number of soldiers we actually had at our disposal, not on paper but in fact. I wanted to know how many men we could use for military purposes. Since I was in that area, I committed myself to carrying out an analysis of the means I had at my disposal in that area at the time. Unfortunately you are not familiar with the events in the battlefield at the time. Have you found that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have a look at it. You can see 21 units with artillery and then it says take away 10 per cent from the total number because of the wounded, sickness, death, et cetera, take away logistics and other auxiliary services, and then it mentions the exhaustion of the people from Jajce unit, from Jajce that had fallen. It says 40 per cent of the Sebastic group also fell. It says they are psychologically ill. Part of the Rodonski [phoen] Group has fled, part of the Bugojno group has fled, of the 5th guard unit only 130 infantry men, then it mentions the Filipovic unit, they have left too. And the Klisa [phoen], they aren't there and then I say, "Fuck it," I don't know how that's going to be translated. Have you ever seen an order of this kind? And when you have a look at me, what do you think? What kind of a situation was I, in the battlefield in relation to command and control and communications, what kind of a state I was in if I conclude my order by writing, "Fuck it"? And this is a report I sent to myself. What's your impression of such an order? Is the commander mad? Is he a fool? Or given that the war has been going on or had been going on for a month and a half in that area alone, people just can't put up with any more, everything is falling apart, so what is the correct impression, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, the impression --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'm going to add another question to the question put to you by General Praljak along the same lines. Let's assume that you find yourself in a similar situation, with 4.424 men engaged with the -- a number of problems or difficulties because about 40 per cent of these men suffer from mental troubles. You're faced with a very great deal of difficulty. According to the standards applicable in the U.K. or in NATO armies, what should military commander do in such a situation? Please answer General Praljak's question first and then my question afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me start, General, by just drawing your attention to paragraph 79 of my report where I conclude by saying that the HVO faced a significant challenge setting up the community of Herceg-Bosna, forming and training an army, and drawing up all the regulations and laws to underpin the HZ HB whilst engaged in an actual conflict first with the Bosnian Serbs and then the Bosnian Muslims, all this would have presented enormous difficulties. I readily acknowledge that. The situation you have just painted is really a from the front example of exactly that. You have in this case whatever it is, 21 units in the Prozor Gornji Vakuf area, they are all of various varying strength, they will be at various states of training, they will be a mixture of regulars and irregulars. They will be some good men, some bad men. There will be some that are prepared to fight and some aren't. But this is where you, as the commander, and we saw a very good example yesterday, giving you a pat on your back for your energy and determination. This is where you, the commander and the chain of command, do their best to try and get a grip of the situation. Not easy in these circumstances. I readily agree. But you will have a chain of command and you've got a huge challenge. I agree that too. Whether that answers the first part of your question, I'm not sure. I could go on, if you want me to, before I turn to His Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer my question: What should a high-level military commander do in a situation where 10 per cent of his men are either wounded, dead or sick, when he's faced with various logistical problems and so on and so forth. What should he do then in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, first of all the commander has a challenge. He is dealing with a very uncertain state. He's dealing with probably a poorly trained force, and he's dealing with a state of some confusion. So the first thing he will have to do is gather in all the information required to make a proper assessment of the situation. He will need to talk to the commanders involved, and then he will need to decide what it is he has to do. Maybe in some instances he might have to disband some units and combine them with others, maybe there are some officers that are completely hopeless. He has to dismiss and put in better officers. There may be logistics issues that he has to address. All of these he will be assisted in by his staff in assessing the information and working out, if you like, the action plan on what has to be done to get to a better situation but that is the role of the commander supported by his staff. In the situation as the picture is painted, this would be serious, it would be demanding a lot of the commander's time. He would be, as he heard yesterday, energetically getting around the front, making his own very personal appraisals whilst his staff was going around getting the sort of detail, logistical situation, and this is where the commander really earns his pay, executing everything he has to do to get his force back on to a better footing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. General Praljak, let me add for fairness' sake that we see that point 10 in this document, that there is a mention of an HV brigade with 230 men. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I can't clarify this now. It's something else but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, have a look at 3D -- there are a few other brilliant orders of mine. I'd like to have a look, 3D 00640. 3D 00640. It's HV or perhaps it isn't HV, we will correct that later on. I don't have the time for that now. General, have you found that, 3D 00640? It's 25th of July again. The Judges know what was happening after the fall of Bugojno and Rama at that time and have a look at item 2. I'm sending this to Petkovic, to General Petkovic because they refused to comply with an order. "Disarm those who do not carry out their order, take off their HVO clothes, arrest them and keep them without food and water until I come back." So it's a commander called Shagway [phoen] who has refused to obey the order. Is this order one that one can understand if one isn't familiar with the situation within which an army commander issues the order? If one isn't familiar with the situation it might seem that an aggressive, sadistic general says keep them without food and water, imprison them, so this would be an example, if you analysed it in this way, of a general who acts in a certain way that encourages soldiers to act in a sadistic manner too, in an inappropriate manner. So is it possible to understand such an order if one does not understand what was happening on the 25th of July in the battlefield? And in relation to General Patton, you know that he almost had to abandon his military career because there was a deserter in a hospital whom he slapped, he said, you're just resting here while your comrades in arms are dying on the battlefield? Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, general, I think that is correct. That's because slapping his soldier was deemed to be against the US military code. Whether keeping them, arrest them, keep them without food and water was in compliance with your own military code, I don't know. But that said, I do understand the order you're giving and I do understand the thrust in which you're giving it, and I would not take that to be sadistic and I would not take that to be setting an example of barbarism that others should follow in dealing with enemy forces. This would be seen much more in terms of a hard-headed commander taking hard-headed measures when necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd also like to say that I did this to some of my soldiers. But let's have a look at 3D 00819, 3D 00819. It's the 23rd of October, its the command of the 111th, the commander, Commander Bozancic, about one year later, well, I granted him four days' leave but have a look at item 2. I say no resignations, no relief from duty, is to be taken into consideration. This is important for the following reason. In a normal army that you served in, you have a commander who for some reason is removed. You bring in another commander because you have sufficient number of commanders, you have the army, you have social security, you have promotions, and so on and so forth. But doesn't item 2 demonstrate something about the HVO? The fact that people simply resigned, a commander of the brigade said, fine, remove me, he had no reason to be a brigade commander or commander of an operative zone, Bozancic said remove me and I said, what do you mean remove you? I can't offer him a rank, promotion, I can't say that his family will be taken care of if he dies, he has to be a volunteer. Did you examine such a way of organising armies on the basis of the documents that the Prosecution provided you with?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I really understand your question. Did you examine such a way of organising armies on the basis of the documents that the Prosecution provided you with? I have the document you referred to me in front of me. I've got paragraph 2, which in my translated one says, no resignments and removals are going to be taken into consideration -- are going to be taken in consideration. I have no idea what this refers to or what the background is. And I don't think I can really comment further on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Praljak, this is un-understandable unless one also has the letter to which it reacts, and it would be very helpful if you could let the witness and the Chamber see the letter to which you refer here. In these laconic expressions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, could you tell us the context in which this letter was sent by you to the commander of the 111th brigade? What was the background, the context?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was just asking whether on the basis of the documents we had and that the Prosecutor provided, that contrary to what other armies did, in our situation, the problem was how not to accept somebody's resignation, because people would hand in their resignation, they would say I don't want to do this anymore, I'm going to go. But I'm just trying to arrive at the truth about what that army was really like. Commander Lozancic says, "Go on, relieve me of my duties, remove me," and I can't do that, first of all because I have nobody to replace him and nobody wants to take on the job. So, as you said, we will be showing a number of documents and my behaviour in situations of that kind, the various threats and so on, and with my theatre and Shakespeare endeavours, well, I like to take it to that level but anyway, P0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Praljak, I asked you very specific question: Where is the letter to which this responds? If we do not see it, this is completely worthless. You are telling us this and that, it may be Shakespeare, it is not evidence because you are not here now talking as a witness. What you tell us, the Chamber must ignore. So where is the letter of 23rd October of Mr.-- whoever it was who wrote it because his name is not even here. There is no name here. We do not know to whom this is addressed, command of the 11th -- 111th XP Brigade Zepce but where is the name? We do not know whether it is addressed to Lozancic or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, there are two problems here: I haven't got the letter right just now, but from what I'm writing here, the other thing is quite clear. I'm writing to Lozancic to say that I wish him to have a rest of four days, and then I go on to say that I'm not going to accept any resignation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I can read what's written here, Mr. Praljak, I am literate. I can read this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, and that's how -- and then it says solve the problems. The third point is solve the problems but I look for the letter, I'll try and find it, but quite obviously somebody is tendering their resignation here and I do not accept that resignation. That's what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, Mr. Lozancic is the commander of the 111th XP brigade; is that right? Is he the commander? So now we understand better.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, take a look at P04 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we'll continue later on because it's now time for to us stop and we'll have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we shall resume the hearing, and Mr. Praljak, you can go on now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Praljak, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, just for you to gain a better insight, I'd like to go through a number of documents, the first is P04207. P0 -- and P04207. The date is the 15th of August 1993. And I'm writing to the president of HZ HB, Mate Boban, and the Main Staff, and I'm in fact asking Mr. Boban what was happening to the people from Grude. We had agreed that they should come to take over their shift and they hadn't arrived, and then I asked what had been done about the deserters from Grude as per the list, and I'm asking them to be brought in, lined up before me, within 24 hours. Now, I don't need your comments straight away. I'd prefer us to look at some other documents first and then when we've seen them all I'll be asking you my question. 3D 01097 is the next document I'd like you to look at, please. I'm the signatory and I'm writing to the Livno brigade, to Commander Vrcoc personally and the Posusje brigade. Last warning because of failure to carry out orders. It's like a warning when you haven't paid your electricity bill, I'm afraid that's what we had to resort to, a last warning, a warning, then a last warning and so on. And it says, the orders of the chief of the HVO GS on sending you Prozor are not being carried out. We are wondering within which military system you are operating. And then it says that the commanders as the most responsible persons will be replaced and criminal proceedings instigated against them. And I demand that you submit a report on the implementation of this order, one after the -- after the events had been sent, and three the post office in Livno is to be -- so that our military lines may operate because they would switch the post office off. Now, 3D 01099 is the next document I'd like you to look at. 3D 01099. And it is the chief of the Jure Rupcic Brigade writing to his commander, the commander of the operative zone of the rank of corps or division and says, "In relation to your order, I herewith report, where do you get the nerve and courage to order something? If I wanted to correspond with you, I would have to come down to your level intellectually and morally, you idiot, which is something I certainly don't want to do." Then let's look at the next document, 3D 01100. 3D 01100. I signed the document and once again, I say that a written report is to be sent to me, why he failed to carry out the order, so to the Klis independent battalion, and then it says this order shall be carried out immediately, unconditionally, and without question and report to me on this, et cetera, and then it says under 3, the commander shall be responsible to me for the execution of this order. And the next document 3D 01101, the next document in line. Here we have it. That's the last in that set of documents for now, once again I signed the document sending it to Valentin Coric. The Petar Kresimir, the 4th Brigade Livno, the 2nd Light Battalion, and I say regardless of everything immediately send a brigade group or whatever from the Petar Kresimir, the 4th Brigade which were in Rama, and find men civilian police, home guards, and other brigade troops, to send them to the lines, the lines that these others will leave. And the commander of the Brigade Stanko Vrcoc and Zdenko Andabak are personally responsible for the execution of the order. There you have it, General. And there is a post scriptum, it says just try not to implement this order. So that's a threat from me, just try not obey the order. You're smiling. Well, the vast majority of those courageous young men whom I had the honour to command, who were decent men, fought honourably, adhered to the laws and regulations, but take a look at these documents and tell me whether you could have ever written anything like this in your professional career, people not carrying out orders, and you're wondering what you can do about all this. So what control is there and what was the realistic possibility for undertaking any sanctions or punishment? Have you ever come across a situation like this in the 40 years of your service and what comments can you make? And I see you were smiling.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, General, fortunately, I have never come across a situation like that. But, then, I've never had the misfortune of being part of a very hastily thrown together army subject to those sorts of problems. It goes back to what I said in my report in terms of one has to understand the conditions that the HVO were operating in. And clearly, you were having enormous problems with -- certainly with the specific people mentioned in these reports. What you subsequently did about it, I don't know. But I suspect you probably would have appeared on their headquarters door step with an escort of military police and taken them away. And replaced them. I don't know. But if you're making the point that life is difficult, life was difficult, and it was difficult to execute command, I would readily understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, General. There is another problem and this is how I'll put my question. Did you ever learn of a situation as follows, on the basis of the documents. You say I appear there, or I say I appear there, I'm shouting breaking things, and taking certain people into custody and bringing them to prison. But what should you -- what would you do if they thought that it was better for them to be in a prison, incarcerated, rather than having to go to the front line, to the battlefield? And you throw them in prison and they say, right, fine, we are happy to say here? What would you do then faced with a situation like that? May we have your comments, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would seek another more effective commander to put in their position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. But you have used the conditional, you would endeavour to, et cetera, or if you used the conditional, I would endeavour to. But the question is as follows: You saw a list of people that the HVO Main Staff had 35 of them, and there should have been 105, so if you thought that the HVO had 50.000 then the Main Staff with all the attending services, based on the kind of establishment you had in Britain, must have had several -- ought to have several hundred people, whereas the HVO just had 35 which is just 30 per cent of what at that point in time should have been the case, and my question is: Who would you bring in if you were to relieve of duty those other people, and if you only had 30 per cent, 35 per cent of the men you needed any way, so if you were to release those who would you bring in?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, it's a hypothetical question but let me give you a hypothetical answer. If you find yourself with insufficient commanders of good standing, then you may be faced with a requirement to start combining units so you have fewer units to command commensurate with the fewer good officers that you have. But hypothetical question, hypothetical answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, quite right. A hypothetical question and a lovely answer. And to test the hypothesis further a group of soldiers from Grude wants to be subordinated to a commander from Livno in view of their domicile, municipality and all the rest of it. Now, from the documents that you were provided by the Prosecution, were you able to draw the conclusion that General Petkovic or me changed 11 brigade commanders, 11 of them? We went through 11 brigade commanders in the space of a year and a half, 11. In Rama, Rama. Once again, from the documents that you were provided by the Prosecutor, were you at all able to arrive at the conclusion that in the one and a half years, General Petkovic and me asked the commander, Mate Boban, to replace 11 commanders of the brigade in Rama, two were killed but the rest were replaced?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that from the documents I read, but given the situation you're describing, that doesn't surprise me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you cannot conclude on the basis of the documents you were given how many I, because I'm talking about myself, how many people I asked Boban to replace? You weren't able to learn about that on the basis of the documents you had?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you said it doesn't surprise me. Could you explain why it doesn't surprise you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the picture that the general is describing now, Your Honour, and the documents that he's showing, are presenting a situation of some confusion, some lack of discipline, some lack of training, some lack of cohesion, the like of which could be described perhaps as the direct result of trying to throw a military force together from scratch very quickly and conduct operations at the same time. So under those circumstances, life for the commanders would have been challenging to say the least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Praljak. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just a few more clarifications. In the operative zone, the Neretva River Valley, southeast Herzegovina, that operative zone, from the documents you were shown, were you able to conclude how many officers who had previously been in the JNA were in command on that territory or some other territory in Tomislavgrad, for example, within the HVO, whether in the brigade zone or the operative zone? I'll help you out. The Capljina brigade, well, can you answer that? Based on the documents you had, did you know how many? Could you know how many in Tomislavgrad and Mostar, that area, in the brigades and operative zones, how many people were in command who had previously attended training in the JNA, the military academy, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understand your question. From the documents I was given, no, I can't give you a number, but I did make the point in the documents that where there were officers that had previous JNA training, they would be generally of a high quality, well-trained, and trained to the JNA doctrine which was really the subject of the report. That's the point I made in the report. How many of them there were there, I can't tell you. Perhaps you could tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you know, for example, that the commander of the operative zone Siljeg was in the Yugoslav People's Army which meant he was in charge of a battalion, he was a captain or in command of a company and was given an operative zone and Mica Lasic was the commander of another operative zone, he was not in the JNA. And of all the brigades that were there, there was another, Obradovic, who was leader of the Capljina Brigade. So of the 13 brigade commanders and operative zones, we had two or three officers and a corporal from a Canadian army? Was that something you could have devised on the basis of the analysis?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in detail and in numbers. I'm conversant with Glasnovic, who was a corporal in the Princess Patrica's Canadian Light Infantry and an ex-Foreign Legion sergeant, I believe. So numbers, no, but I go back to the point I just made where there were officers with JNA training, they would have been of higher quality than others. It was the point I was making.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yesterday we had a problem, the Prosecutor gave you a document where you could see that part of the artillery was controlled by the Main Staff, whether the chief of artillery or myself or somebody who was on duty there. Now, do you know that that part of the artillery was exclusively from the Mostar operative zone Pocnikvo [phoen] the artillery of Posavina, Central Bosnia, Tomislavgrad, they had no links and there was no control from the Main Staff because of the distance. So the part of the artillery that you looked at yesterday, as being under the control of the Main Staff, related to the artillery in only one operative zone, that is to say the Mostar operative zone?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware that it was only available in the Mostar operative zone because I would have concluded that you would have been able to move it to other zones, particularly zones that were cohesive with HZ HB and not like Zepce or Vitez, having to cross into factional boundaries. If you chose not to move the artillery, then obviously there were going to be problems about supporting places like Tomislavgrad which were out of range.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me. Did you in any way -- were you able in any way on the basis of the documents to conclude --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please check the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were you able in any way to conclude why the Main Staff for a time took a portion of the artillery and placed it under its command? The artillery belongs to the corps generally speaking, so why would this have happened?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
