utterances.text: Well, as I said yesterday, I made the assumption that scarce assets and long range assets which were not widely available but which would be useful to be able to reinforce others were held centrally and that's why you did it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much more time do I have, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have used up one hour and eight minutes. You now have seven minutes left, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, please, General, regardless of the fact that war is a total social -- well, terrible things happen during a war, but can we say that wars -- there is -- are differences between wars, there are wars that are revolutionary wars, or civil wars, or religious wars, or wars between states, ideological warfare and so on? Would you agree that there are different types of wars, liberation wars, wars -- defensive wars and so on?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, yes, I'm happy to agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My next question is this: Since were you in Bosnia-Herzegovina and studied all this, would you agree with me that the Yugoslav People's Army in 1991 and 1992, in defending its constitutional provisions, carried out an aggression both on -- against Slovenia and against Croatia and against Bosnia-Herzegovina? If you can't tell me, you can say that you don't want to deal with those matters but otherwise, would you agree with me that that was so?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were talking about the international laws of armed and the Geneva Conventions yesterday, I made the point that these were really drawn up in the aftermath of state on state wars, and I went on to make the point that there will inevitably be intellectual and legal debate on how you define what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina and how the Geneva Conventions drawn up for different circumstances were applicable and I went on to make the point that the -- the base line was common humanity. So whilst there are different forms of wars, I can't comment in detail on how you would actually define what was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some people have described it as civil war. Some people have described it as interfactional war. Some people have described it as interstate war. I will leave the Court to decide what sort of war that was. But I return -- I would return lastly to drawing your attention back to the doctrine on international laws of armed conflict, where there is a statement which was read out yesterday that it applied to any form of war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: General, it's not my intention in any way whatsoever, because of the form of a war, to deny the right which applies to every armed person and every group of people and so on. That's not my aim. All I asked you and you've answered me in part, whether war, after an aggression, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, can be considered both a civil war and a religious war, and I'm going to ask you this for the following reason. The BH army, for instance, it used the term "Allah-U-Ekber" when it attacked some positions, whether the of the Serbian army or the HVO, and that all the people killed in the BH army were Shehids, that is to say they fell on Allah's Road. So they didn't lay down their lives for their nation or their state, but on Allah's Road, Allah's Course, and that's what is said and written today. So were there elements in that war, both of a civil war and a religious war, would that be correct that there were those elements there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That war comprised in the main three ethnicities, Serbian, Croat, and Muslim which became known as Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Unfortunately, my time is running out. Otherwise, I had prepared an analysis of various civil wars, the Spanish civil war, the American Civil War, and of course the French revolution, in part, but regardless of whether laws -- well laws should always hold true and rights too, but civil wars with elements of a religious war where the army and the people are mixed up, whereby definition far more bloody with far more civilian casualties then classical clashes between two armies in some other kind of war, is it more difficult to control this type of war, are the consequences more serious, is the method of warfare far more complex with a far more emotions, fear, poverty, in every civil war, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, I would agree with your general thrust there, and I have alluded to that in the report I wrote. The situation facing any of the three sides or two sides, whichever way you want to look at it in whatever time frame, was highly complex, full of emotion, and as such, the commanders and the chain of command on each and every side, having found themselves in that position, carried enormous responsibility, heavy responsibility, to ensure in whatever way they could that the war was conducted as far as they could ascertain and ensure in a manner that would be in accord with international laws.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last thing I want to ask you, 3D 01102 is the next document. 3D -- it's the last document. 3D 01102. It is a document which was compiled by the OTP as a final report about what happened when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was bombed by the NATO forces, and over the problems of Kosovo. I'd like to ask you to look at page 3 of 21, page 3 of 21 pages, which lists the most important incidents and categories of targets. It is paragraph 9 actually. Would you look at paragraph 9, please? So it was the OTP that compiled this report when it was thinking about raising an indictment against NATO forces, and then it changed its opinion because it was seen that these were just -- there was no intent, it was just chance occurrences, but if we look at A, B, C, down to S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you just said something that surprises me, you said that the OTP had the -- drafted an indictment against NATO. What do you base yourself on to say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there was a problem with the interpretation or translation. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, the microphone is not switched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak used the word looked into, [B/C/S spoken], looked into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even if you say that they had looked into it, how do you know about it? Were you present in the Office of the Prosecutor itself? How do you know that they envisaged that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents was taken from the IDS system of the Tribunal and that's what it -- the title says. It was on the internet published a long time ago. We saw it in the Kordic trial. It was publicly announced and accessible to the public. It was in the newspapers, published in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Scott had kept silent for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I've been trying, Your Honour, very much so, and succeeded up until now. I'm sorry I didn't succeed for the whole day frankly because I intended to, but I won't be able to keep that promise to myself, I suppose. It's unfortunate that I rise now because of this particular document because the Court might perceive or some might perceive that I have any interest in obstructing any relevant, and I emphasise the word "any relevant" discussion of the document. However, I do know that we are on a very tight schedule, I know Ms. Alaburic has made her concerns very loudly and well known based on the time limitations, and I do think that the general has used his time, and I assume that Ms. Alaburic would like to have as much time as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please complete your cross-examination as quickly as possible, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we have a list of points and the least number of civilian casualties as collateral damage is listed, collateral damage, which of course there was no intention to -- in this, but 500 people were killed, innocent people, with all the sophisticated up-to-date army, I don't want to impute any intention there, all I want to say is this. If we look at the number of possible errors by the NATO alliance, the number of mistakes that occur in Iraq, for example, under conditions that can't be controlled, or the number and what happened when the army to which you belonged waged a war in the Falklands. And when outside the area that was proclaimed a war zone, the Argentinian Belgrano ship was sunk with 300 members of the crew. So in modern warfare, with the highly sophisticated military organisation that this involves, does it exclude the relatively high number of civilian casualties on the basis of these documents in the Iraqi war, for example, and the example I've just quoted of the Belgrano in the Falklands war? May we have your comments, and I'll end there. That's the last question that I have.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just pondering how to articulate a coherent answer to your question, but I can't let your allegation on the Belgrano slip by. The Belgrano was a battleship, and it was interstate war, and it was sunk by a UK submarine, nothing to do with civilian casualties. So let's move on. I've never seen the document you have shown me. And I can see what it's getting at. And I note that this report does not mean that in every case the site in question was deliberately struck by NATO. The point you're making is in modern warfare are civilians at risk? And the more that -- and so I would answer that in terms of if -- if the form of warfare is to use a modern expression, war amongst the people, then it is one of the sad consequences of that form of war that the people are going to be at risk and that in itself puts much greater onus on commanders to do their level best to ensure that the -- that the people, in inverted commas, are not harmed inadvertently. That is not to say that on occasions, civilians will not find themselves in the line of fire. That is the nature of war and that is what has always happened. But that is quite different from a deliberate intention to attack civilians. So if I've answered your question, I think I'll leave it at that, unless you'd like me to amplify it in some other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We should stop now because your time is up, General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. Thank you for your answers. Thank you for appearing here, and I'd like to thank the Judges too and also the Prosecution for not having interrupted me on this occasion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd like to greet Your Honours, General Pringle, and my colleague Scott. Mr. Scott, who has expressed his understanding of the interests of the Petkovic defence. Before I start my cross-examination, I would like to thank the Chamber for explaining that an hour is sufficient for the cross-examination of this military expert because his report is of a normative kind. I'd like to inform the Chamber of my position, that in the light of that explanation, I believe that my right to cross-examination has been curtailed, at least my right to cross-examine with regard to the factual basis and the documents that the expert report is based on. And then secondly, my rights have been curtailed with regard to the subjects addressed by the Prosecution in the course of their examination-in-chief. Thirdly, with regard to the documents that aren't contained in the report but were shown to the witness over the previous two days. Fourthly, in relation to the thesis of the Prosecution in the course of the examination-in-chief with regard to certain events and certain documents. Fifthly, in relation to the witness's answers to questions put to him by the Prosecution in the course of the examination-in-chief. Six, in regard to the questions and subjects or issues raised by judges when putting questions to the witness, and if I may I'd also like to point out how important a certain subject is, and Judge Trechsel, as is often the case, raised this important issue. The issue is whether the HVO Main Staff can be considered to be the supreme commander's staff. Had we had enough time to deal with this issue, which in my opinion is of great importance, it would be possible for us to determine the rules or rather the Decree on the Armed Forces in the HZ HB which states that when carrying out staff, the staff work of the Supreme Commander, the Main Staff of the HVO shall be established. We could also see how the General Staff in the JNA in wartime conditions is transformed into the Supreme Command staff. The seventh subject in relation to which I believe my right to cross-examination has been curtailed concerns the objections raised by the Judges to some of my objections, which I can raise in the course of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I can't let you say that, you say I'm not entitled to cross-examine the witness. You have one hour to put all the questions you want to the witness. Whilst you were talking, I've reviewed 20 documents. Whilst you were talking, I could have submitted 20 documents to the witness to get his opinion about them. Please proceed. No one prohibits you from putting your questions. You have one hour to do so. One hour to put the most significant questions to the witness. I can -- I could show you that with your case file, I could review all the documents in one hour with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can express understanding for your position, but I had to point out that I don't believe be this position you have expressed is correct. I stand by my objections. I believe that an hour is not sufficient for me to cross-examine this military expert. There are no examples at this Tribunal that the Defence of an accused is granted one hour for the cross-examination of a military expert. We have no such cases in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, General, allow me to introduce myself, my name is Vesna Alaburic I'm a lawyer from Zagreb, and together with Mr. Stewart, a lawyer from London, I am representing General Milivoj Petkovic, whom you have referred to in the course of the last few days and he was a JNA officer, and I would like you to be aware of the fact. I would also like to tell you that the Petkovic defence considers your expert report a logical one, a commonsensical one, and one the scope of which is universal. And we have no intention to bring any -- or to cast any doubts on any of your conclusions. We regret the fact that we don't have sufficient time to deal with some of your comments on the confusing situation that prevailed in the territory of Herceg-Bosna. We won't have the time to discuss the problem of poor training, of local massing of people, the lack of local military means, because we believe that all these elements contribute to weakening the effective control of military commanders. So much for my introduction, and now allow me to put my question to you. You have a bundle of documents before you. We don't have the time to go through or to read through those documents. If I refer to some documents, I will refer to them hypothetically, I will present certain hypothetical situation to you, and I will ask you your opinion in relation to that hypothetical situation. Since you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1995, tell me, at the time, was the HVO considered to be a legitimate army that was part of the army of the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in Bosnia in April of 1995 and was there until end of October, I think it was. At that time, the HVO and the Armija were -- had come together in the -- as the forces of the federation, as I have to say somewhat uneasy bed-fellows.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: For the benefits of the Judges, if they want to verify this, they can have a look at 4D 4826. General Pringle, if someone gives you total freedom or gives you as much money as you need without any strings attached and gives you the possibility to engage any officer or any soldier that you know, in that case, in such a hypothetical situation, and I'm talking about founding an army, you have everything that you can have, that you need, to found an army, so in your opinion how much time would you require from the time the decision on founding an army was taken until the time at which the army would be prepared to function? In accordance with the well known NATO doctrine.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the first instance of course it would depend on how big an army you are intending to raise and the resources you can put in to raising and training it. In passing, the American army expanded from 100.000 to I think a size of 4 million in about four years. So let me see if I can be a bit more helpful. The basic training of a soldier would probably, in peacetime conditions, probably take up to, say, six months. You could probably train a soldier in an intensive crash course much quicker than that, and you could probably do that in about three months, at the end of which he would be competent to be a functioning infantry soldier. To train the specialists like gunners, rocket people, communicators, would take longer. Do you want me to stop there?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you could, could you tell us how much time you would need for certain operations that precede the training of soldiers? Because in order to start training soldiers, a precondition is to have the facilities in which you will train them, you'll have -- you need to have the officers who will train them, you need to have all the logistics that are required. If we assume that you have nothing and that you need to find the facilities, training personnel, and equipment, how much additional time would you need to train the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, answer dependent on the size of the army you're trying to form, but if you really are presenting a scenario where you're starting from scratch, you're going to have to first of all recruit the trainers and then train them, and then you get the trainers to train everybody else. So that would take time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately how many years one would require until the army can start functioning in accordance with NATO doctrine? What is required for the chain of command to be established, the communications line, the possibility of introducing disciplinary measures, the founding disciplinary courts, how much time would it be -- would be needed to have all the elements of a regular army? We had a foreign officer here who said that in his opinion, one would require approximately ten years. Could you say whether you would agree with that or was that answer a correct one?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're painting a very, very hypothetical situation in that you're painting a situation where something is starting from an absolute clean sheet of paper. Of course, you know, NATO armies have been in existence in some cases for many hundreds of years, and they are not starting from a clean sheet of paper so that instance has never arisen. I can see where you're coming from and probably where you're going to. To create a fully functioning army with fully functioning headquarters and fully functioning equipment and fully functioning doctrine from scratch on a clean sheet of paper would take several years. I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General Pringle, have you ever heard about the concept of All People's Defence when you were examining JNA doctrine? Do you know what this means?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe All People's Defence was the requirement for any citizen of the former Yugoslavia to bear arms in defence of his country in the event of foreign invasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether one of the elements of All People's Defence was the principle of territorial organisation, so certain military units were established in certain municipalities, they were formed of the people who were citizens of those municipalities and their task was to defend their municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that is correct, and indeed I can give you a bit more flavour on that in that one of my Bosnian Croat interpreters used to amuse me by telling me that part of her school syllabus was AK 47 weapon training.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, we all used M 48s. I have no idea what an AK 47 is, though. General Pringle, on the basis of the HVO documents that the Prosecution provided you with, did you come to the conclusion that the HVO was also organised on the basis of this idea of municipal brigades?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm hesitating because in general terms, I'm alert and aware to that. I was wondering whether I could recall that in the Decree on the Armed Forces. I'm not sure if I can recall that but in general terms, I understand what you're saying and I'm aware that that's how it was organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's assume that there is no doubt about the fact that the HVO was established as municipal brigades which then linked up on a regional level and on the level of Herceg-Bosna as a whole, but could you tell me whether this would mean that the HVO was in fact organised on the basis of principles that were valid for the All People's Defence system?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe such an organisation is -- would probably have been derived from the All People's Defence system and would have preceded HZ HB and is probably -- and was probably the system in use by the former Yugoslavia when it was one state.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, would it be logical to draw the conclusion that the HVO was established as a defensive army, an army that was to defend certain municipalities in the territory of which a brigade had been established?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the HVO, I think we -- I would agree that the HVO was established as an army, whether it could be described as a defensive army and whether the implication is -- on that is it only defends itself and doesn't attack, I think I would have more difficulty in agreeing that but certainly the HVO was -- appeared to be established as a functioning army and as with all armies, their principal and first function is defence of the homeland.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. I would now like to deal with an important subject, a subject that is important within the context of command and control. It's a subject you have referred to on a number of occasions, General. You told us that a commander should monitor the implementation of his orders, and if he establishes that his orders haven't been carried out or haven't been carried out as they should have been carried out, in such a case, such a higher level commander should relieve his subordinate of his duties and bring someone in as a replacement, someone who would carry out the orders in an appropriate manner in future. Have I understood you correctly? Is that what you in fact said?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with that. I would only amplify it by saying that it -- this is not the commander functioning solely alone. The supervision of the implementation of the orders and the assistance of the implementation of the orders is also very much a function of the commander's staff, and the commander's staff is reporting back to him in addition to the observations that the commander is making for himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's try and clarify this immediately so there are no future misunderstandings between us. If I have understood your expert report correctly, and if I have understood the JNA documents correctly, on the basis of singleness of command, anything that a single member of staff has done is considered to be the act of the commander of the unit within which that staff is located; is that correct? In other words, that commander is responsible for the acts of his -- of his associates and for other chiefs of staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commander executes command based on the authority vested in him by law. As such, the commander is responsible for everything that happens in his command. He is assisted in the execution of his command by his staff, who issues instructions on his behalf and in his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's the clarification I wanted. So General Pringle, in future, when I say commander, I also mean his associates and his entire staff. Let's go back to the subject of appointments since this is important if one is to have effective control, tell me, in your opinion, is it the right of a commander to appoint and remove his subordinates or rather is this right one of the important elements when it comes to ensuring that he has effective control over his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in general, but the process you would expect to find laid down in sort of documentation or doctrine dealing with discipline and appointments, so a commander -- there may be a process of review committees, for example, that assess a wide range of officers and select that officer for a particular appointment, so the commander would not have necessarily selected him. If, having been appointed, he is found to be woefully inadequate, invariably the commander has the immediate right to remove him, but then that then has to be processed back through the system of how, why, and where he's going to then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Pringle, I would like -- I would now like you to make yourself acquainted with the rules for appointing and removing officers in the HVO. This will probably be the only document that I will refer you to. On the very top of my bundle of documents, you have the instructions -- for the Judges, they are instructions for the use of my binder, the top, there are four sets of documents I have decided to use for my cross-examination, if I have the time. As for the other documents, well, this was the consequence of my optimism. I was thinking I would have five hours for cross-examination. Document 4D 828 is an amalgamation of documents. General, just have a look at the title page, where you can see the rules or a summary of the rules on appointments and removals in the annexes or attachments you have documents that show that this summary is correct, and you also have attached individual orders from President Mate Boban, so this concerns individual orders, and you have Tihomir Blaskic's orders. He was the commander of the Central Bosnia operative zone, and he had special authority when it comes to appointing and removing individuals in that operative zone. I believe these things are of much importance. General, Please listen to me, I think what I tell is going to be sufficient, according to the rules in force in Herceg-Bosna, brigade commanders and commanders of operative zones, so these are the highest level commanders of military units, were appointed by the president of the Presidency of the HZ HB. Then there was a lower level of officers who were appointed by the HVO for one period of time, and then by the chief of the defence department, and what is also important is to point out that brigade commanders had the right to appoint and remove platoon commanders and commanders at lower levels, as I said the commander of the Central Bosnia operative zone had the right to appoint any one in his operative zone throughout the time period relevant to the indictment. If I could just add an explanation for Judge Trechsel, under 2D [as interpreted] you have a lot of orders of Tihomir Blaskic that are referred to and that's because we want to show that during the entire period relevant to the indictment he had such authority because on one occasion a question was put as to whether this was in force only for a short period of time or throughout the time period. I'd like to correct something in the transcript, page 61, line 11, it's not 2D, it's item 2, 2. General Pringle, if you look through these rules, trust me for the moment, the Judges will be able to examine the rules subsequently and see that what I say is correct, but the HVO Main Staff according to these rules didn't have the authority to appoint a single commander of a military unit. In your opinion, does this fact affect the possibility for the HVO to have effective control over subordinate commanders of military units?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the rules in front of me. And I said that would be an appointment and promotion possess, and this is plainly the process in HZ HB where particular people are authorised to appoint and dismiss officers of various ranks. What it doesn't say is would the president of the HZ HB Presidency, in appointing commanders of brigades or high-ranking officers, I mean in the written word there you would assume that he's doing that entirely by himself. Whether he is actually doing it in consultation and discussion with his most senior military officer is for debate but that's what I would expect, and similarly, the Croatian Defence Council appoints and dismisses commanders of battalions, platoons and et cetera, and I would expect there also to be a military input into the consultation prior to appointing and dismissing. When you get further down the scale, brigade commanders have the authority to appoint and dismiss various levels, yes, I -- that's what it says, but whether they are doing that with no reference upwards or discussion, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Pringle, well, that wasn't the substance of my question either. I know that you don't know about the actual events, so I'm not asking you how military commanders were appointed. I'm just asking you on the basis of these rules whether in your opinion the fact that the Main Staff of the HVO based on the rules and regulations, has no role in the appointment and relieving of duty commanders of military units, to influence the possibility for effective control. Does this influence their ability for effective control in an area? I'm asking a hypothetical question again. I'm asking you in principle. And the question is not about whether that control actually existed and whether it was put into effect.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When you're talking about the Main Staff, I assume you are referring to the commander of the Main Staff rather than the corporate body of staff officers. If I read the rules literally, there is no mention there of the HVO Main Staff. Whether the commander of the HVO Main Staff had any input to these decisions and appointments, I don't know. I'd be surprised if he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. As you're not a witness of fact, we won't delve into that. I'd like to move on to another area now, General Pringle. Before that, a brief introduction. The Prosecutor yesterday presented a thesis of his backed up by several documents and questions that he asked the witness. And this is what that's about. In showing document number P3019, which is an order from General Petkovic dated the 30th of June 1993 on disarmament and isolation of Muslim soldiers in the HVO, and then by asking the question about securing logistics, logistical support, General Pringle, listen to me, please, General Pringle, are you listening?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may not be looking at you but I can assure you I am listening to you. I was actually looking for document 3019 while listening to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to ask you anything about the document. That's why I didn't ask you to look it up. But the question of ensuring logistical support for accommodating several thousand Muslims who would be isolated, and then in showing you document P4756, which the Prosecutor did, and those are the minutes or a report from the Defence department senior staff meeting of the 2nd of September 1993, and finally, in showing you a document P4841, which is the record from the government meeting of the HVO, of the 6th of September 1993, the Prosecutor put forward the following thesis: That the head of the Defence department recognised the authority of the Defence department over the Ljubuski and Heliodrom prisons, and that the government on the 6th of December -- 6th of September 1993, said that authority does not fall on the government, from which he offered up the thesis that for everything that went on in the detention centres in July and August, it was my client, General Petkovic, who was responsible for it or rather, General Praljak from the time he became the commander of the HVO. Now, Mr. Pringle, it is my task and duty to show that this is a completely incorrect thesis on the part of the Prosecutor, that it is a construction of his which contradicts the exhibits in the case so far, and also other evidence which the Prosecutor planned to introduce into evidence during this trial. So I'll start off with that and see how far we get with the time we have at our disposal. Now, the subjects that I'm going to deal with are to be found in the following --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me Your Honour, I'm trying to minimise my interruptions this afternoon but just so there is no mischaracterisation of -- well, I mean, sorry. I didn't mean that in an intentional sense, but lest the Prosecution position be misunderstood, my friend just said that it was the Prosecution thesis that for everything that happened from basically the end of June forward in connection with the detentions, that it was Mr. Petkovic. There may be some suggestion or put it implicitly that only Mr. Petkovic was being argued was responsible for that. I can assure the Chamber that's not the Prosecution position, and of course we believe that to one degree or another all of the accused are responsible for that conduct, not just Mr. Petkovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, I'm now briefly going to quote the documents that I wish to refer to and those who have the documents could take a look at them. So without doubt, my client on the 30th of June 1993, wrote an order, which among other things ordered the disarmament and isolation of soldiers of Muslim ethnicity in HVO units. Later on, we'll look at the causes, but let's see what happened on that day, the 30th of June 1993, what happened on the territory of the whole of Herceg-Bosna, and what the other organs and structures of Herceg-Bosna were doing in terms of defence and security for the territory of this community. Now, from a document, one of the many reports by foreign observers, European observers, the number of document is P3025, we can see, General, well, I'd like to tell you what happened on the 30th of June 1993, first. On that day the BH army attacked the HVO barracks in the Mostar area on the left bank of Mostar. Its name was north bank or the Tihomir Misic barracks, Bijelo Polje, Vrapcici, and other areas north of Mostar. The HVO lost control over those territories thanks to the treachery of the Muslims in the HVO who acted in favour and in cohorts with the BH army. So this was treachery on the part of the Muslims in the HVO. They were traitors. In the Mostar region, there were HVO units in which the Muslims at that point in time, that is to say June 1993, made up 35 or 40 per cent of the overall number of soldiers. Several months prior to that, the percentage was even higher, it was as high as 55 per cent. And the question presented itself: If unless -- something was done with respect to those Muslims, there was the danger of the HVO losing control over all the territories which the HVO had under its control, in which the Muslims were members. So the question was what should be done, what to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on that day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm reluctant to be back on my feet again, but now we seem to be getting into an area if this is being put to the witness as a hypothetical question and Ms. Alaburic is postulating these things as a hypothetical question, I suppose we can leave it to the general to formulate his answer. However, if it's meant to be a statement of the evidence or a neutral statement or something that the Prosecution would be expected to agree with, of course we don't. We don't accept the characterisation that what happened was due to the quote "Treachery of Muslims in the HVO." We don't accept that all Muslims in the HVO engaged in that. There is a number of assertions in the question, just so the record is clear, the Prosecution does not accept.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I haven't come to my question yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you were setting out the premises for your question for the last five minutes. Every time you ask a question, you spend five minutes introducing a whole series of data, and it's very difficult to follow them. And furthermore, Ms. Alaburic, you are relying on an international document that I have, and while you were speaking, I was looking at this document. The attack by the ABiH according to this document was attributed to the fact that this was an attack for survival because of the very bad situation that there was in East Mostar. Now, what you were saying doesn't come out of this document. You say I'm going to ask a question on the basis of this document, but then you add in other aspects. So it's very difficult to follow you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like your observations not to be counted as part of my time, and I'd like to look at point 5, section 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was related to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then without any explanation, I'd like to refer you to point 5, section 5, where the betrayal of Muslims in the HVO is discussed. It is a subject that we have brought up with at least 15 witnesses [Realtime transcript read in error "minutes"] and the Petkovic defence considered that this was a topic which the Trial Chamber had already had knowledge of. And as far as Mr. Scott's intervention, I would like to say that I haven't come to my question yet. Now, as to the length of my question, I would like to say the following. If I wish to receive an answer from the military expert about a hypothetical situation, hypothetical because he is not a factual witness, then that hypothetical situation has to be explained by me otherwise we can all go home, and we have nothing further to discuss with this witness. However, do I consider that this witness has a lot of knowledge and that it is a great pity for this Trial Chamber and indeed for the trial as a whole that we have not been able to use him, if I can use the term, in his full capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, let us assume that what I described happened as an event on the 30th of June, and I'd like to draw your attention to the following documents which we are not going to tender now, so I won't waste time reading through them, but the document -- these documents show clearly that the president of the HVO reacted as did the head of the defence department in ordering a general mobilisation, that the order was sent on down to all the defence departments in the municipalities of Herceg-Bosna, and that the order was handed down to all the brigade commanders, and that on the 1st of July, the head of the chief of the military police issued an order connected to the order I mentioned on mobilisation and an introduction of a curfew. In brief, what I want to say is this, and I'll come to my question later on: That all the organs of Herceg-Bosna at that point in time did what they could in order to protect the safety and security of the territory of Herceg-Bosna. Now, tell us, General, please, on the assumption that what I have just said is correct, is it logical that the organs of Herceg-Bosna would do everything in their power to ensure the security and safety and HVO control over the territory that they considered to be Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You started by talking about the order that was given to round up the Muslim community and Muslim soldiers in the HVO, and the point I made yesterday was not whether that was right or wrong, understandable or not understandable. The point I made yesterday was that if that was going to happen, there were severe logistic consequences that should be taken into account in order to make sure that the people could be held in reasonable conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so. Precisely. I agree with your conclusion on the need to ensure logistical support, but I'd like to ask you the following question. The fact that something like that was done without previously ensuring any -- securing any separate buildings or special security or food storage space, does not all that go to show that there was no plan in place for incarcerating and isolating Muslim soldiers in the HVO? In your opinion would that be the logical conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my opinion, at that time, from the document I read, there didn't appear to be a preplan to do that. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the third group of documents or set of documents, at the top of my binder, you will find documents which show what the authorities of Herceg-Bosna in fact tried to do in order to solve the problem of the incarcerated HVO members who were Muslims first of all, because at the beginning of July, they were the largest group. I'd like to draw your attention to some of those documents, the ones that I consider to be most important. I think a permission granted by Valentin Coric, who was head of the military police administration, the document is P3292, on the 8th of July, he approved to the High Representative of the UN organisation for refugees to visit three localities where detainees were being held. Now, tell us, General, on the basis of this permission granted, is it indubitably true and correct that the HVO authorities ensured foreign -- the representatives of foreign humanitarian organisations to become informed of the fact that the Muslims were being held and were being informed of the conditions of detention that these Muslims found themselves in?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Referring to your document 3292, what it actually says is, "Are hereby authorised to pay one visit only." If you pay one visit only, you get an impression of what you see during your one visit only, and what happens after that you have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct, General. But from this authorisation, does it emerge that the HVO did not hide the fact that there were incarcerated Muslims and that in fact the HVO enabled representatives of international humanitarian organisations to go and see for themselves what the situation was like and that they asked for assistance in dealing with those detained Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, the document does permit one visit of the UNHCR to the Heliodrom, not that -- not that the detention of the Muslims in my opinion would have been secret because it was being well covered, I believe, by the media and was well known to be happening and indeed was being observed by foreign observers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, not to waste too much time, whether it was one visit or not, well, it's clear that it was one visit here but let's assume for every visit this kind of authorisation would be issued, and let us also assume that authorisation was given to every international humanitarian representative and that the international humanitarian organisations were informed of the fact that a large number of Muslims, Muslim soldiers of the HVO, were in detention. Can we agree with that as something that we are not challenging, as an indubitable fact?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's take it as an assumption and let's see what the question is you're going to follow the assumption with.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, from this authorisation, is it quite clear that they were coming to assess the situation and whether any humanitarian assistance needed to be given or not? So was this visit in order to ensure humanitarian aid to the detained Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that that -- I can't say -- I can't agree with your last sentence because it doesn't say anything here, but the UNHCR is involved with and has responsibility for exactly that and you would expect a UNHCR representative to be taking stock of the conditions in a camp and reporting back and doing what they could to alleviate the situation as well, and in addition, you would expect the Red Cross to be doing very similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, please, how do you interpret the final portion of that authorisation on the need to provide -- to assess the need for humanitarian aid as it says, in order to assess the need for humanitarian aid, the last part of that sentence in the authorisation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said that is very much their function, is to take stock of the situation and decide what support would be required, and to try and work out how, whether, and when they could get it through which in itself would require various sort of authorisations and permissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let's look on 3560 is the next document, P0. It is a report of the 19th of July 1993, and look at the last part of the document, item 7, conclusions. Would you take a look at point 6? And the entire item relates to prisoners. Item 6. To make contact with representatives of the high commissioner for refugees with the aim of opening a transit refugees centre under the auspices of that international organisation. Let's assume, General, that the contact did take place, they did make contact, and that the authorities of Herceg-Bosna did indeed try, in cooperation with the UNHCR, to resolve the problem of the detained Muslims, HVO soldiers. Can you agree with me when I say that the problem of detention was something that the authorities of Herceg-Bosna tried to solve in cooperation with international humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, plainly the issue is on the agenda of the defence council minutes, and I agree that paragraph 6 at the end is calling for the establishment of contact with representatives of the UNHCR in order to open a transit refugee centre under the auspices of this international organisation. They are trying to get the UNHCR to open, it would appear, some sort of transit centre. So, yes, I can agree that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, General, let's look at the situation that existed prior to the 30th of June 1993, and I apologise to Their Honours for showing some of the orders that we've already looked at here and are already exhibits, but General I should like to ask you to focus on the documents in the fourth set of documents in my binder. So section 4 in my binder. They are documents of the BH army which relate to the way in which Muslim HVO soldiers were treated and some of the cautions issued by some of the Herceg-Bosna services about the danger because there was a large number of soldiers within HVO -- Muslim soldiers within HVO units, and General, on the assumption that everything is correct, what the documents say, I'd like to hear your expert opinion on the security situation under those conditions. The first document that we have is 4D 00469, which is an HVO document, let's start off with that, the date of it is the 30th of March 1993. It is the crime department, and the second bullet point in the introduction says that the HVO service cautions that pressure is being put on Muslims who are members of the HVO and MUP units to leave those units, and if they fail to do so, they are threatened that they might be killed or their houses set on fire. Since we don't have enough time, I have to move on to the next document straight away. And that document is 4D 473 -- no I apologise. Let's start off with 4D 33, 4D 33 and look at the third bullet point from the bottom -- from the bottom. The document is from the chief of security of the 42nd Mountain Brigade of the BH army, who says, and I quote, "That all the Muslims, members of the HVO, must be called to take the side of their own people." Now, the next document, document 4D 34, that same person, on the 18th of April, says, in the third line from the bottom, "That cooperation should be established with our soldiers in the HVO and that the seriousness of the situation should be pointed out to them." Now, document 4D 35 is next. Point 2 there says or rather the last line of point 3, by Bajro Pizovic the commander of the mentioned brigade of the BH army, establishes that the department for morale and -- well, moral guidance and training will devise a plan for informing the troops about the composition of the brigade, the population on the territory of Mostar municipality as well as Capljina and Stolac and Muslim soldiers who are to be found in the HVO units of the municipalities cited. Now, document 4D 36, dated the 2nd of May 1993, is the next one we'd like to look at. Commander of the 4th Corps of the ABiH in item 3, it says -- 4D 36. It's the second half of item 3. It says, "The men from the HVO in Capljina has the task to take the village of Vrapcici and the bridge in Capljina. And they should not allow forces to be brought in from the direction of Matkovic." And two lines later it says, "For taking -- seize the town of Stolac without people in the HVO." 4D 568, have a look at 4D 568. The chief of the security department of the Main Staff of the Supreme Command of the ABiH, the last sentence, "It's very important to prepare ourselves for such a situation and to inactivate the Muslims who are in the HVO and to exercise influence on them to move from the HVO to the army of the RBiH." Have a look at 2D 150 now. It's a Defence document. It's a Stojic Defence document. It has to do with looking at the ethnic affiliation of HVO members, the ethnic membership of those members. This is dated the 9th of June 1993. We'll see what the situation was throughout a certain period of time. The document has no information on Central Bosnia as such information was not provided, so it doesn't concern the entire territory of Herceg-Bosna. In the municipalities mentioned here there are a little under 6.000 Muslim soldiers and in the Mostar area, the area of the 1st and 2nd Brigade, there were 35 per cent and 20 per cent or rather over 2.000 Muslim soldiers. We can also have a look at some Prosecution documents. You also have them here. P1438 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please ask your question because we need to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I won't read through the other documents, General. I want to draw your attention to these ABiH documents which show that the ABiH directed its activities to Muslim soldiers in the HVO. Tell me, according to the information you have, would a HVO commander, having found out about such ABiH documents, would he have believed that Muslim soldiers in the HVO posed a certain security threat, posed a danger?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can understand that he would.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I suggest we have the break and then I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to break. We'll have 1 hour and ten minutes left. I know that Mr. Prlic has 15 minutes. I have the feeling that the other counsel gave their time away. Mr. Karnavas, are you going to use your 15 minutes or have you given them to Ms. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I did not give my time to Ms. Alaburic. I believe that Coric team does have some time, and I am reserving my time in the eventuality that I might need to use. I mean, there are some areas. But I am flexible. If you're running out of time, I think I did much of my questioning through my interventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take note of this. Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President we have granted our 15 minutes to the Praljak defence. We keep the right to use 15 minutes. It depends on how things unfold. We are flexible. Perhaps we won't need them, but at this point in time we believe we will be using that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we haven't granted our time to anyone. We have half an hour but at the moment I don't believe we'll need that much time, but I can't be certain until later on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Ms. Alaburic, you'll have ten minutes after the break because you've used 50 minutes so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you have ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I continue, I'd like to correct something in the transcript. Page 67, line 20, I did not say that we had discussed that subject for 15 minutes. I said that we had discussed about the subject with 15 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, we have very little time. Let's try and use that time to clarify some details. Have a look at a document in the Prosecution binder, P00586.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 586. 586 in the Prosecution binder. I don't think the Prosecution has the lurid colours that the Petkovic Defence has or the bright colours, rather, that the Petkovic Defence has. But perhaps you could concentrate on my words. This has to do with the structure of the Defence department. It was read through by my colleague, Ms. Nozica yesterday. Please comment on part of item D, the last section, paragraph, where it says that the brigade commanders are subordinate to and accountable to the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as the supreme commander of the armed forces. I'll skip the continuation of the sentence and my question is as follows, General. On the base of this sentence, can one say that brigade commanders were subordinate and responsible to the supreme command of the armed forces? Was that as a rule the case? If we could have this on the e-court system, it is item 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there is a misunderstanding. It says section D like delta. What you mean was B like Brno or Belgrade or whatever you like. Budapest.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 5 in the English version. Item 9. I didn't say B or D at all. That's why I didn't understand what you were saying. So it's section B, item 9, the last paragraph. It says, "Brigade commanders shall be subordinate and responsible to the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as the commander in chief of the armed forces, and to the head and chief of the Main Staff within the scope of their responsibilities in accordance with the powers described above." It's not very clear in the Croatian language, but for a start, General, with regard to the first part of the sentence, would you interpret this as saying that brigade commanders are subordinate and responsible to the president of the HZ HB who is at the same time the Supreme Commander of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that to be laying out the chain of command going from the bottom upwards, brigade commanders, chief of the Main Staff, president.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you comment on this part, brigade commanders shall be subordinate and responsible to the Supreme Commander and then to the chief of the Main Staff in relation to certain other elements? In your opinion, what justifies such subordination and such responsibility? What justifies the fact that the brigade commanders are subordinate in this twofold manner?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the president of the Croatian community is, I believe, also the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But if could you comment on this I'd like to know why reference is made to brigade commanders here, first they are subordinate to the Supreme Commander and then in certain circumstances they are subordinate and responsible to the chief of the Main Staff, given the experience you have had, how would you interpret this given your experience and knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but I do think this is a relevant point. For some reason when looking at that section, everyone seems to be dropping the reference to the head of the Defence department, which is not at least in the transcript that I've seen, we're talking the Main Staff, we haven't been talking about the head of the Defence department, that is Mr. Stojic, also in that same chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if we are going to go that route, I suggest that we also look at the entire page, the way it's written. The first paragraph talks about administrative tasks, the second paragraph talks about strategic and operative plans. I think there is some -- there lies some major differences. I think those need to be explained before we go even further. And I don't know whether the gentleman is competent at this point in time,, I'm not saying in the sense not intelligent or about whether he has studied the document well enough to opine on that. But I think if we are going to go through this particularly with respect to what Mr. Scott indicated, I think we need to analyse the entire page word for word, para by para, sentence by sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm grateful for all these instructions, but yesterday this entire item was read out by my colleague, Ms. Nozica. I wouldn't now like to include the head of the department in this because I think this could just complicate matters for us, and I don't have the time for clarifying matters. I want to clarify this two or three-fold situation in which commanders are subordinate and responsible to certain individuals. Brigade commanders are responsible and subordinate to certain individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, have you ever seen such a -- such provisions? Could you interpret them if you have? Because it's very important for us in this case.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about this document yesterday. And we also talked about the chain of command and we talked about unity of command, and I read this document without going right from the top, but as laying out the chain of command from the president as Supreme Commander of the armed forces down through the chief of the Main Staff, down to the brigade commanders. You wouldn't expect a brigade commander to take orders directly from the Supreme Commander bypassing levels of command in between. That would lead to complete confusion. And that would transgress the principle of unity of command. Have I answered your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, that is the sort of answer I wanted to get. You have just said what it would mean if the Supreme Commander issued direct orders to brigade commander and bypassed the Main Staff. Tell me would your conclusion be the same if the Supreme Commander issued orders to commanders of operative zones without the Main Staff being aware of this or rather by bypassing the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we talk about brigade commanders and operative zones, and I'm not sure if an operative zone consists of a number of brigades or whether a brigade consists of a number of operative zones. I think it's the former. But to talk sort of hypothetically, if a senior commander is giving orders to a junior commander skipping out levels in between, without keeping the levels in between informed, then that will lead to confusion. In fact it's dangerous. On occasions, skip echelon command, if you like to call it like that, does happen for reasons perhaps of speed or security, but if the intervening levels of command are not kept informed, as I say, it's dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, please have a look to document in my set of documents, 4D 576. It's a document from the commander of the Central Bosnian military district from Tihomir Blaskic, 4D 576.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that section 4?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No. It's further behind. It's in the -- it's among the single documents, the documents that haven't been grouped or placed in categories. Could the usher provide assistance? It's at the very end, General. It's not part of the groups of documents. It's at the end, 4D 576. It's a report from the commander of the military district or from the former Central Bosnia operative zone. It's to the Supreme Commander. We won't be dealing with the contents of the document. Have a look at the beginning of the document, when it says, "Subject, tasks, I was given in the office of the Supreme Commander on the 28th of September 1993 between such and such a time." And at the end of the document, you'll see that it was forwarded to certain institutions, and there is no doubt that this document was not forwarded to the HVO Main Staff. This document shows that the Supreme Commander directly assigned tasks to the commander of the Central Bosnia military district. General, assuming that that was in fact the case, are we dealing with a chaotic or confusing situation that you referred to a little earlier on?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it does seem to be an order -- referring to an order from the Supreme Commander. I don't know whether the Supreme Commander has talked to the chief of the Main Staff or even whether he was there when he gave the order, so on the face of it, it has -- it doesn't appear to involve the chief of the Main Staff, but I can't say -- I can't say -- I can't comment on why.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Naturally, you can't, but I'm just interested in knowing the following: Under the assumption that this is in fact the situation, is this an example of the confusing situation that results when one skips a certain level of command?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is what has happened in this case and the chief of the Main Staff is not alert to the order, that would be the sort of example of what I was talking about earlier, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the document that comes before this one, 4D, 575?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you give me the time, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... D575?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've used three extra minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is an example of direct communication between Mr. Blaskic and Mr. Boban. Please pay attention or have a look at item 2 where it says, the Ahmici case has been concluded in accordance with your instructions. Tell me, are you familiar with the Ahmici case? Do you know what is being referred to here? So as to not waste any more time, have you heard about it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there was an atrocity carried out at Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does this document show that the Supreme Commander issued instructions as to how to deal with the Ahmici case and Tihomir Blaskic, the commander in Central Bosnia, was to carry this order out? Can we agree that that is the case?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can agree that it appears to be an order direct to Blaskic, who, as a point of -- a point that may be pertinent, at the time, I believe, was cut off from the main body of HZ HB and it may -- that may account for some of this skip echelon going on because the chief of the Main Staff probably didn't have too much authority over him. But I don't know. That's an assumption. But it may strike a chord.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mrs. Alaburic would you be so kind as to recall to us what ONO is, a copy goes to ONO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the operations and training department. It's a department that filed all documents, it dealt with documentation in a certain sense. I don't know how else to put it. It's a -- let's say an archival unit, an archival department in a certain unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is it with the General Staff or with the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Each and every military unit and command had their own ONO, operations and training department, so when we present our case, you'll see that within the structure of each and every command, and that includes the structure of brigade commands, there is always an officer for ONO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Ms. Alaburic, we have to give the floor to Mr. Pusic and to the Prlic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I naturally have other questions for this witness. I have to complete my cross-examination now because I don't have any more time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, I thank you and I do regret the fact that we didn't have time to continue. It would have been useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The Coric Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, General. Good evening to everyone in the courtroom. I only have a few questions that I would like to put to you. On a number of occasions in your report and before this Chamber, over the last few days, you emphasised the importance of training. I'd now like to link up to something that my colleague, Ms. Alaburic, asked you about. She asked you a question about an army that was being established. You have an infant army, you're starting from scratch, and let's assume that such an army doesn't have trained officers, trained instructors, it doesn't have professional staff to train its soldiers. So let's take this hypothetical situation. In such a case, would the responsible person, the military authorities or the civilian authorities or certain military commander, would such a person act logically if he asked for assistance from the outside or, rather, from outside his army, if he, for example, sent his officers abroad to be trained there? Or would it be better for him to bring instructors to his country from abroad, instructors from countries that already exit -- instructors from armies that already in existence and have the adequate knowledge? Would that be a logical procedure to follow?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are putting a hypothetical question about a hypothetical country which hypothetically alludes to a legal -- certain legal status, but under those hypothetical conditions, yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If I've understood this correctly, I think I have, your report was compiled on the basis of documents that can be seen at the end of your report in the annexes. Those are the only documents that were you given by the Prosecution, am I right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you another question. We had a look at a document which you can find in the Prosecution binder. We could bring it up on the screen too, but I don't think it's necessary. I think we'll be able to remember the document. It's a Prosecution document P04020. It is an order issued by General Petkovic dated the 8th of August 1993. Item 1 in brackets, it says, "That the military police is responsible for utilising prisoners." I only have one question about that. Among the documents that you have examined, do you remember having found any rules, any laws, or decisions stating that the military police administration is responsible for utilising prisoners? I've been through all these documents and I never came across such a thing. Do you remember having found anything of this nature in any of the documents that you examined?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I seem to recall reading that one of the -- that one of the duties of the military police was the guarding and dealing with prisoners. Which document that was, I don't know. But it is in all armies pretty standard for the military police to have amongst their responsibilities responsibilities for prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I wasn't asking about security. I was asking you a question about use or utilisation. That's the word that bothers me. So "use" or "utilisation" in the sense in which the term is used in item 1.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it may be a translation, but I read this "Ask the authorisation through military police administration, (in charge of utilising prisoners) as meaning that the military police administrative branch has amongst their functions the coordination and ordering of the -- everything to do with working the prisoners." That's how I would read the word "utilising" there. I don't know how literal that is in translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: My question concerns the part that says fortifying the achieved lines and the word "utilising" is being used within that context, in relation to fortifying the lines.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read that. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, my question is whether you found that the military police was authorised or was responsible for authorising someone to be taken away to fortify the lines? Did you come across a statement to that effect in any of these documents that you examined?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems to be apparent here in this order from General Petkovic, where it says fortify the achieved lines immediately, that's the order, prisoners and detained Muslims may be used for fortifying lines. Those are the means. And ask for authorisation through military police administration who are in charge of utilising prisoners, seems to be the method.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Yes, but did you see any other documents, documents of a general kind, I'm not asking you about any particular orders, did you come across any other documents that regulated matters in this manner?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I wouldn't expect to come across a document that said -- that says that part of the military police's function is to use prisoners in fortifying lines in the front line because that is in direct contravention of the international laws of wars, so I wouldn't expect to find a document laying that down.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask you about. That was in fact my question. But I probably didn't phrase it precisely enough. I have another question I'd like to put to you. Yesterday, something was discussed with you that I don't think the subject was sufficiently and precisely defined. We were referring to the duty of a commander to punish inappropriate behaviour, whether such behaviour was crime, violation of discipline, et cetera. And you told us that after a commander finds out about such an act, about a violation or a crime, it is his duty to take all the necessary steps that he can in fact take, so could one say that a precondition for an officer, for a commander, to punish a subordinate, is that he has been provided with the necessary information or rather that he knows, in fact, that he's been informed of the fact that a certain act or a certain crime has been committed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commander receives information through a whole host of different fashions, through reports, through radio communications, through television or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: You've already told us that and I understand that. I understand all that. He can receive it in a hundred different ways. But the precondition is that he must have received the information. Now, what way the information reached him is another matter, but he has to have the information. He must know about it. That's all I'm interested in. That's all I'm asking you now.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me if a commander does not know of an event, can he take action on it, the answer is no. The supplementary issue is for how long does he continue not to know of the event because as soon as whenever he does become aware, he then has a duty to take action. So it's common sense that if he doesn't know for whatever reason he can't do anything, but when he does become aware, if he becomes aware, then he has to.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Don't mind my asking you this next question, I'm not a military expert myself, nor do I have military knowledge apart from the fact that just like everybody at secondary school, as in the former Yugoslavia, I did have lessons in All People's Defence and social self protection but that's where my knowledge remains, but prompted by your discussion with General Praljak during today's sitting, I think he should have gone on to ask you another question which is this. I'm going to ask you this now. With respect to the disobedient officers, when you said that there was not enough officer cadres, then the commander had to pool his men and then he would need less officers if he were to group his men in that way. And that would resolve the lack of officer staff and troops in general. Do you remember saying that in that general discussion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put forward a thesis that to me as a layman seems logical. If there is a permanent state of war, that is to say that there is combat on a daily basis, that fighting is going on all the time and that communication has been cut off with other territories or the communications are poor, that under such conditions, it is difficult to inform the new officers about the situation on the ground prior to their arrival, and if the lines are dispersed, not only do you have very few troops to cover those lines, but -- well, anyway, would all this make it impossible or make it much more difficult, given this kind of situation, to realign the army and transfer people if you have a war going on all the time, with fighting going on all the time? Would that make it even more difficult and well-nigh impossible, that is to say to apply the approach that you put forward?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're conducting reorganisation in the middle of the war yes, that's difficult, but that's what commanders are paid for.
