If they have to reorganise units in the course of operations, which is not unusual by the way, that's what they have to do. So the fact that there is a war going, may make it difficult, may make it challenging, but that's what commanders are there for.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: But apart from the disobedient officers and the deserters and everything that we discussed previously that's another situation that makes it more difficult, what I've just said, it's additional difficulty?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: War is difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions but with the Trial Chamber's indulgence, I'd give the Coric Defence five of my minutes or rather Mr. Coric would like to ask questions himself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. General, you touched upon affairs relating to the military police and that was my wartime assignment. Do you understand what the military police administration actually means, the concept, the term? Can I assist you? It is the top-most military police organisation, which numbers several thousand people, the military police is to be found in the brigades, the operative zones and so on and so forth. So is that how you understand it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took it to be the top-most sort of staff branch, if you like, of the military police predominantly in charge of the -- what I would describe as the regular military police rather than the ones who are not or were not originally full time military police but are now called military police who are to be found down at brigade level where they are locally raised, for example.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with you absolutely. Now I'd like to return to the order which mentions that permission for people to be taken out to do work, to do labour, but that is something that the military -- the police administration deals with. Would it be impractical for a broad area like that, that any unit in the operative zone, for instance, must have to refer back to the military police administration to be given permission to take the prisoners out for work? Would that be practicable?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that depends on locations and communications. I would -- I take it we are talking about the Mostar area and the events are happening in the Mostar area. So I don't necessarily see that that's that difficult.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we are dealing with Mostar, but what about Rama or Central Bosnia? And I do say that there are no orders or provisions as General Petkovic dealt with it. It might appear, so if anybody has seen anything like that they can show it, but as the number 1 man in the military police, I say that there was never an order like that or provision like that, and if the military police administration is mentioned in this document, would it be logical that this document was sent to the address or to the attention of the military police? Because throughout the document no mention is made of any of the military police branches, let alone the military police administration, so this document must have been sent -- should have been sent to the military police or the commander, or do you agree that that ought to be so, ought to have been so?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got the document in front of me any longer, but if I remember it rightly, the recipient was being asked -- the recipient was being invited to round up a number of people, using military police from whom -- and to get the authority from the military police administration who I assume had had that task. So I would think we are talking about quite a local incident, and I'm not sure I've got the thrust of your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry that you don't have the document in front of you now because I don't think you're interpreting it correctly, but let's go back to basics while you're looking for the document.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: You have it, right. As the most responsible man in the military police at that time, I state that the military police did not have the task of deciding about whether somebody was going to go up to the front line and do work there, et cetera. Counsel told you that in --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, my apologies, I know time is short, but you just can't simply have one of the accused standing up and asserting a factual proposition as if it's true. It is the Prosecution's case of course that the military police administration was centrally involved in the approving and directing of the use of prisoners and forced labour, and with all respect to Mr. Coric, he can't simply stand up and say that's not the way it was. If he wants to take the witness stand some day and say that, I'll be happy to cross examine him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'm going to take up the question that was asked rather in an unfortunate manner. In any military system, is it conceivable for the head of the military police, number 1, has absolutely no powers to send prisoners that are held either in military prisons or else in detention units guarded by military police, to the front lines? Is that conceivable or not? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the head of the military police is abiding by the laws of armed conflict, under no circumstances would the head of the military police authorise the use of prisoners on front lines, under no circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We said we would be flexible when it comes to the expert report aspects of control and command, it is Mr. Pusic's position that there should be no questions in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas? The last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good evening, you Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone in and around the Court. Given that the gentleman's remit as I understand was to do a general analysis of the three Cs, command, control, and communications and give than he's admitted that he's not an expert on the HVO, has not been to the field, does not know how many officers were there, what their actual numbers were under any given circumstances, I don't think that it would be necessary for me to conduct any cross-examination. I take the gentleman's word that he's not an expert on the HVO per se, as it existed at that period of time. We do wish to thank you for coming here, and we do wish him good luck in his future endeavours and safe travel back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I didn't expect to have any time, but I think I just have one or two questions for the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just this, I think. General we spent considerable time today talking about the creation of an army, and I think sometimes various people have used it starting an army from scratch or from a blank sheet of paper. Can I just ask you if you're aware of the fact that in the countries of the former Yugoslavia, or that is the former Yugoslavia itself, that all -- all men were subject to mandatory military training and a period of military service?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that, and indeed the system of All People's Defence has been discussed this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So to that extent in fact you would not be starting "from scratch"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe the raising of this particular army was starting from scratch. It would have been starting from a position of widely varying trained ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And once again thank you for coming to The Hague and providing us your considerable expertise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to thank you for having come here to The Hague to answer the various questions over three days. I know that this is the third time you've been here. You've already appeared in two previous cases. And I hope that you will not have to come a fourth time. I would like to express my very best wishes for your return trip. I will now ask the usher to take you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just one little thing related to the transcript and your earlier question, perhaps I should continue in Croatian. I'm sorry. [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 32, line 18s to 20 of the transcript you asked about P43 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker kindly repeat the numbers, please, more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: A unit was mentioned in that document which was HV. You said HV. Or rather, HV Hrvatinic -- the number of the document let me repeat is 4235. Mr. President, you asked what the initials HV meant. I checked the document out. It is the name of a local unit from Prozor, it's not HV Croatian army. It's a unit from Jajce, I apologise. It's the name, Hrjvoje Vukcic, HV. No, I wrote it down. Hrvoje Vukcic Hrvatinic. It's a character from the 14th century, Bosnian Croat nobleman. So it's quite clear that the text under number 9, Hrvatinici has nothing to do with the HVO or HV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for spelling that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, just to -- again to respond to one of the Chamber's previous inquiries, Mr. President, you asked, I believe yesterday, concerning the full translation of a document, the attachments had a number of diagrams and boxes and that has been provided to you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have it. And thank you for it. Next week we will meet at quarter past 2 on Monday. There is a witness expected to appear. I don't know who will be carrying out the cross-examination. We will be informing you by e-mail of the distribution of time allocations, and you will be aware of those tomorrow morning at the very latest. So see you on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 12th day of November 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 25
